idiom_name: hand-rolled hash table keyed by row id (uthash) owned by the session
implementation_notes: C has no ORM session, so the classic structure is the whole realization: a hash table (uthash's HASH_FIND/HASH_ADD over a UT_hash_handle) keyed on the row id, owned by a session struct, with the loader inserting on a miss and returning the shared pointer. Because uthash keeps structures in place, the instance address stays stable and callers can compare and share pointers; clear and free the table when the unit of work ends. The classic form is always justified in C - there is no framework to absorb it - but a process-global table is the anti-pattern to avoid.
pitfalls: uthash does not enforce key uniqueness: check with HASH_FIND (or use HASH_REPLACE) before HASH_ADD, or a second load silently creates a duplicate entry.
Keys must not be modified while hashed; identity fields are stable only if loader and updater agree never to change them.
uthash has no locking: a table shared between threads needs an explicit mutex, and the session struct must own clearing/freeing or rows leak past the session.
